articles.title: Here’s What Your Seat Choice Says About You, According to Flight Attendants
articles.content:
作为一名特别抠门且对拥挤有超高耐受力的乘客，我很少会额外付费选择座位。但如果有机会选座，我一定会选靠窗位置，毫无争议。我喜欢靠着墙壁休息，把帽子拉过脸来，假装自己是个被轻轻摇晃入睡的卷心菜（在一个闻起来像汽油和脚臭的摇篮里）。这让我感到很舒服。而我的丈夫则更偏爱过道座位，因为他患有严重的"坐不住病"，无法在一个小时内不起来"活动一下腿"（换句话说，就是在走廊里溜达并与陌生人闲聊）。

我们结婚这么多年，这个问题从未解决过。但看来，我们或许根本不需要解决！根据空乘人员的说法，我们从一开始就注定会选择这些座位。而且，事实证明，我们还不算是最奇怪的——令我惊讶的是，夫妻分开坐竟然是一种非常常见的现象，而且往往是故意的，原因我们稍后再谈。你的座位选择真的能透露出很多关于你的信息，因此我联系了几位空乘朋友，询问他们多年来对乘客和座位选择习惯的观察。让我告诉你，他们的答案绝对让人眼前一亮。

原来，你在飞机上选的位置竟然是一个相当可靠的窗口（抱歉），可以让人一瞥你的性格、应对压力的方式，甚至是在每小时500英里的速度下，你的婚姻运作模式。那么，你最喜欢的座位究竟透露了什么？请系好安全带，继续阅读。

根据我采访的空乘人员，除了语言风格和鞋子款式之外，座位选择也能揭示一些真相——但有一个重要的前提是：许多人并不是自己选的座位。在爆满的航班或临时订票情况下，人们最终只能坐在剩下的位置上，而非自己理想的座位。但当乘客有选择时，一些模式就会自然浮现，空乘人员注意到这一点，因为他们每周都在观察成千上万名陌生人做出相同的决定。

西德尼·A.是一名资深空乘人员，她在美国四大航空公司工作了20多年，她说这些模式足够一致，以至于她通常可以通过快速扫视登机的乘客，大致判断出他们会坐在哪里。"我无法解释，但从性格上来说，我能知道谁会坐在哪里"，她告诉我。她还发现，商务旅客倾向于选择一个特定的位置（稍后会详细说明），而整个家庭似乎本能地聚集在某个区域，而非受航空公司政策的影响。洛蕾塔·H.是杰特蓝航空的空乘人员，她指出金钱也起着一定作用。支付额外费用升级座位的乘客也往往会在飞行中花费更多。"看起来，坐在更贵座位的乘客会更自由地花钱，在推车经过时购买东西"，她说。"坐在后排的乘客通常不买食物或额外物品。"这提醒我们，座位选择并不纯粹是心理问题，也是一个实用问题。

不仅仅是空乘人员有看法。当《读者文摘》在Instagram上就"过道 vs. 靠窗"进行投票时，评论区变成了一个温和的争论场所，而人们给出的理由几乎与空乘人员告诉我的完全一致。当然，这些内幕知识不仅仅是给机组人员的鸡尾酒会谈资。它实际上有助于他们更好地工作，稍后我们会详细讨论这一点。但首先，让我们进入有趣的部分。

无论你是过道党、靠窗党还是接受命运的中间座乘客，你的偏好座位都能透露出你的优先级、压力水平，或者在某些情况下，仅仅是你的内裤尺码。以下是空乘人员观察到的情况。

**过道座位**

过道座位的乘客倾向于重视效率和便利性而非舒适度。西德尼说这类人群中商务旅客占比较高，他们希望能不受干扰地工作。"我注意到商务人士通常会坐在过道位置，因为这样更容易打开笔记本电脑，需要起来做事时也更方便"，她说。这也有助于他们更快地赶往会议或连接航班，因为可以更快地离开飞机。选择过道座位也可能意味着你不喜欢麻烦他人……或许还有点控制欲过强。西德尼也承认自己属于这一类："我希望能在需要时立刻起来，而不必请求旁边的人不断让路。"

我们的Instagram跟随者补充说，他们选择过道座位的原因与我丈夫类似：活动空间大。"过道，每次都选。我们可以偶尔起来走走"，一位评论者写道。另一个人则更直接："过道……而且我最后登机，这样就不会被其他乘客碰到。"一位跟随者用一句话总结了整个控制因素："我希望能站起来而无需醒来或向任何人道歉。"

**靠窗座位**

如果你是靠窗党，恭喜你：你可能是一个睡眠爱好者、飞行爱好者，或两者兼具。"对于喜欢睡觉的人来说，他们确实更倾向于靠窗座位"，西德尼说，因为有墙可以靠，而且不会有人在你睡觉时爬过你。如果你醒来了？窗户就在旁边，可以欣赏到地球的壮丽景色。靠窗座位也适合有健康焦虑的人，因为它让你远离高人流量的过道，这也是为什么洁癖者和焦虑症患者常常选择它。这里也有一种不同的控制欲。"靠窗，这样我可以控制遮阳板……我想在飞行时观看风景"，一位评论者告诉我们。确实，靠窗座位让你可以决定周围人的光线强度，这对那些喜欢掌控自己体验的人很有吸引力，即使有人在驾驶飞机。

我们的Instagram评论区中的靠窗座位忠实拥趸也像过道党一样热情地陈述他们的理由。"靠窗！内置头枕，方便小憩！"一位评论者写道。几位频繁乘客坦言，他们的偏好会随着航程长短而变化："短途飞行：靠窗。长途飞行：过道"，正如一位跟随者所说——这证明即使是铁杆靠窗党也可能在长途飞行时投靠过道。

**中间座位**

没有人梦想坐在中间座位，空乘人员也确认了这一点：这通常是无奈之选，而非性格宣言。但谁会坐中间座位以及如何被填满，能透露出周围人的很多信息。西德尼注意到一个特别甜蜜的模式，许多夫妻中："丈夫会礼貌地让妻子坐过道或靠窗座位"，她说。"我经常看到这种情况。"她补充说，年轻夫妻几乎总是订购连座座位，即使知道其中一人必须坐中间。不太迷人的则是一些年长夫妻的行为，他们会订购同一排的过道和靠窗座位，让一个完全的陌生人被夹在中间。"这会让中间的人非常不舒服"，西德尼说。"很尴尬。"如果你曾经坐在两位明显相互认识但却对你不理不睬的乘客中间，那么现在你知道原因了。他们可能已经结婚30年，只不过需要一点个人空间，好吗？

为了维护我丈夫和我的名誉，我们从不试图让其他人感到尴尬。我们的理想是能有一个空置的中间座位，这样我们就能有更多空间。不过，如果你是故意选择中间座位的人，你可能是个反社会人格者。开个玩笑！但你可能非常回避冲突——比如让别人坐你的靠窗座位，而你选择中间座位以避免争吵——或者你只是喜欢与陌生人交谈，过道座位给了你两次搭讪的机会。

**关于身体条件和预算**

这与性格无关，更多是关于身体条件和预算。"高个子是我见过最在乎自己座位的人"，西德尼说，他们通常会付费选择额外空间的座位，无论是应急出口排还是其他升级的腿部空间选项。洛蕾塔也同意身高比任何深层心理控制需求都更重要：她看到高个子（以及有几个额外现金的人）付费选择杰特蓝航空的"更多空间"座位。至于谁倾向于坐在实际应急出口排，洛蕾塔说没有明显的模式：主要是愿意付费获得腿部空间的人。应急出口排座位也有自己的权衡，因为联邦法规要求坐在这里的人必须能够在紧急情况下提供身体和心理上的帮助。

带小孩的家庭和希望最先离开飞机的旅客往往会盯上前排，因为那里提供一些额外的地面空间。不过，值得一提的是，并非所有看起来"宽敞"的座位都名副其实 —— 前排座位的餐桌通常是嵌在扶手中的，这意味着你失去了抬起扶手以获得更多活动空间的能力。

如果你是喜欢坐在机舱前部的人，你可能只是一个喜欢规划且希望快速、无麻烦离开的人。或者，西德尼补充说，你可能有飞行焦虑，更希望靠近飞行员和空乘人员。而坐在靠后位置的乘客则往往对整个飞行过程更加随和——或者他们带着孩子，希望靠近餐车和洗手间。

家庭并不总是坐在一起，这并不是因为他们不爱彼此。是的，你的猜测是正确的：有些父母会故意让孩子坐在另一排，这样旅途中可以有点和平和空间。虽然这对幼儿来说不是个好主意，但作为一位母亲，我可以证明，青少年往往和父母一样喜欢这种安排。但有一件事让我惊讶：西德尼说，整个家庭确实倾向于聚集在飞机的某一特定区域。"在西南航空，我们会在中间看到更多家庭"，她说。"我不知道为什么，但他们似乎本能地聚集在飞机的中间部分。"

除了明显的过道 vs. 靠窗的分歧之外，空乘人员还掌握着许多秘密，并在整个航程中默默观察着一些与座位相关的行为。例如，赤脚放在座位、餐桌或前排座位扶手之间（恶心！）表明你不在乎他人的舒适感，可能社交意识不足。（令人欣慰的是，西德尼说近年来这种情况已经减少了。）

她也注意到人们在发现自己坐错了位置时的反应，无论是错误还是故意，希望没人注意到。有些可恶的人可能被分配了中间座位，但却占据靠窗座位，戴上耳机并忽略真正的座位主人——希望他们会因害怕闹场面而不敢声明自己的位置。"是的，这种情况确实存在"，她确认道。"但更多情况下是无意中坐错位置。"

她的建议是，如果有什么事让你不舒服，不要害羞，可以大声说出来——机组成员宁愿帮你解决问题，也不想让你在整个航程中默默忍受。

机舱观察不仅能让空乘们更好地做好工作——在乘客开口前就预判需求，使整个航班更顺畅，还能帮助他们提前应对各种情况。例如，如果机组人员能预见到紧急出口排的乘客需要额外的安全说明，中排的家庭需要帮忙照看孩子，或者14C座位的乘客一解开安全带就会拿出笔记本电脑，他们就能相应调整服务。这其中还有经济考量。了解谁更可能在机上花钱、花在哪里，可以帮助机组人员提前安排服务。而且，即使没有这些实际好处，显然空乘们也确实享受这一机舱社会学实验，每天都在观察着不同的人。作为一个常常分析家人在路上为何会有某些行为的人，我非常赞赏这一点。所以下次登机时，请记住：一名穿着西南航空制服的空姐正在默默观察你，你确实是一本打开的书。

（原文《根据空乘观察，你的座位选择反映了什么》首发于《大众读物》）
articles.summary:
I am cheap and have an unusually high tolerance for being squished against strangers, so I rarely spring for a seat assignment when I fly. But when I do get to choose, it’s window, every time, no debate. I like to lean my head against the wall, pull my hood over my face and pretend I’m a burrito being gently rocked to sleep (in a cradle that smells like gasoline and feet). It’s very comforting.

My husband, on the other hand, prefers the aisle, because he has a serious medical condition called “ants in his pants” and cannot go an hour without getting up to “stretch his legs.” (Translation: wander the galley making small talk with strangers.)

We’ve been married a long time and have never once resolved this. Turns out, we may not need to! According to flight attendants, we were basically doomed to pick these seats from the start. And, apparently, we’re not even the weird ones—it’s shockingly common for couples to sit slightly apart, on purpose, for reasons we’ll get into later.

Your seat choice really can say a lot about you, so I called up a couple of flight attendant friends to ask what they’ve noticed about passengers and their seating habits over the years. Let me tell you, they did not disappoint. It turns out where you plant yourself on a plane is a surprisingly reliable window (sorry) into who you are, how you cope with stress and even how your marriage operates at 500 miles an hour.

So what does your go-to seat actually reveal? Buckle up and read on.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more travel, cleaning, humor, tech and fun facts all week long.

Is a person’s seat choice really that revealing?

According to the folks I talked to, things like how you speak and your footwear reveal more about your personality, but seat choice can tell you something real—with one important caveat: Many of us aren’t picking our seats. On a packed flight or last-minute booking, people end up wherever there’s an open seat, not necessarily where they’d choose. But when passengers do have options, patterns emerge fast, and flight attendants notice them because they watch thousands of strangers make this exact decision, week after week.

Sydney A., a flight attendant who has worked for more than 20 years for all four major U.S. carriers, says the patterns are consistent enough that she can often guess, just from a quick scan of who’s boarding, roughly where someone is headed to sit. “I don’t know how to explain it, but like, personality-wise, I know who’s going to be sitting where,” she told me. She’s also noticed that business travelers gravitate toward one particular spot (more on that below), and that entire families tend to cluster in one general area, seemingly by instinct rather than any airline policy.

Loretta H., a flight attendant for Jet Blue, points out that money plays a role too. Passengers who pay extra for upgraded seats also tend to be the ones who spend more once they’re airborne. “It appears that people who sit in more expensive seats spend money freely and buy things off of the cart when I come through,” she says. “People in the back usually don’t buy food or extras.” It’s a good reminder that seat choice isn’t purely psychological—it’s also practical.

It’s not just flight attendants who have opinions here, either. When Reader’s Digest polled our Instagram followers on aisle-versus-window, the comments section turned into exactly the kind of good-natured argument you’d expect—and the reasoning people gave lined up almost perfectly with what the flight attendants told me. Of course, all this insider knowledge isn’t just cocktail-party trivia for cabin crew. It actually helps them do their jobs better, which we’ll get into a little further down. But first, the fun part.

What does your seat choice reveal about you?

Whether you’re an aisle person, a window person or someone who’s resigned themselves to the middle, your preferred perch says something about your priorities, your stress levels or, in some cases, just your inseam. Here’s what flight attendants have picked up on.

The aisle seat

Aisle-sitters tend to be people who value efficiency and access over coziness. Sydney says this crowd skews heavily toward business travelers who want to work uninterrupted. “Businessmen and -women I’ve noticed usually sit in the aisle because it’s easier to have their laptop out and get up and do things if they need to,” she says. It also helps them get to meetings and connections more quickly, as they can get off the plane faster.

Choosing the aisle may also mean that you don’t like to inconvenience others … and may be a bit of a control freak. Sydney counts herself in that camp: “I want to be able to get up when I need to and not have to ask the people next to me to keep moving.”

Our Instagram followers added that they choose the aisle for the same reason my husband does: mobility. “Aisle, every time. We can get up and walk every now and then,” wrote one commenter. Another put it more bluntly: “Aisle … and I board last so I don’t get bumped by all the passengers.” One follower summed up the whole control angle in a single line: “I want to be able to stand up without waking up or saying excuse me to anyone.”

The window seat

If you’re a window person, congratulations: You’re probably either a napper, a flying enthusiast or both. “For people who like to sleep, they do like window seats,” Sydney says, since there’s a wall to lean on and no one climbing over you mid-doze. And if you wake up? That window is right there with a gorgeous view of the planet spread out beneath you.

Window seats are also good for people with health anxiety, as they keep you farther from high-traffic aisles, which is part of why germaphobes and anxious flyers often request them too.

There is also a different aspect of control here. “Window, so I can control the shade … I want to look out at the landscape as we fly over,” one commenter told us. And it’s true, window sitters get to decide how light or dark it is for everyone around them. This appeals to people who like to feel like they’re steering their own experience, even when someone else is flying the plane.

The window loyalists in our Instagram comments made their case just as passionately as the aisle crowd did. “Window! Built-in headrest for naps!” one commenter wrote. A few frequent flyers admitted their preference shifts with the length of the trip: “Short flights: window. Long haul flights: aisle,” as one follower put it—proof that even die-hard window people might defect for a long-haul flight.

The middle seat

Nobody dreams of the middle seat, and flight attendants confirm it: This is usually the seat of last resort rather than a personality statement. But how a middle seat gets filled can say plenty about the people around it. Sydney has noticed one particularly sweet pattern with couples: “The male will offer his wife the aisle or window seat, to be nice,” she says. “I see that a lot.” She adds that younger couples almost always book seats together, even knowing that one of them must sit in the middle.

Less charming is what happens with some older couples, who book the aisle and window seats in the same row and let a total stranger get sandwiched in the middle. “It makes the person in the middle super uncomfortable,” Sydney says. “It’s awkward.” If you’ve ever wondered why you landed in the middle seat between two people who clearly know each other but haven’t said a word to you, well, now you know. They’ve probably been married for 30 years and just need a little space, OK? In my husband’s and my defense, we never try to make anyone else feel awkward. The dream is that we end up with an empty middle seat so we can have extra space.

However, if you are the person who intentionally chooses the middle seat, you may be a sociopath. Just kidding! But you may be very conflict avoidant—say, letting someone sit in your window seat while you choose the middle seat to avoid a fight—or you may just love talking with strangers, and the aisle seat gives you two opportunities to chat someone up.

The exit row or extra-legroom seat

This one’s less about personality and more about anatomy and budget. “Tall people are the people I see the most that care about where they’re sitting,” Sydney says, and they’ll often pay for the extra room regardless of whether it’s an exit row or another upgraded legroom option. Loretta agrees that height plays a bigger role than any deep psychological need for control: She’s seen tall people (as well as people who just have a few extra bucks) pay for JetBlue’s Even More Space seats.

As for who tends to sit in the actual exit row specifically, Loretta says there’s no strong pattern beyond that: It’s largely just people who want the legroom and are willing to pay for it. Exit row seats have their own trade-offs too, since federal rules require anyone sitting there to be able to physically and mentally assist in an emergency.

The bulkhead seat

Families with small kids and travelers who want to be first off the plane both tend to eye the bulkhead, since it offers a little extra floor space up front. It’s worth knowing, though, that not every “roomy-looking” seat lives up to the hype—bulkhead seats often have tray tables built into the armrests, meaning you lose the ability to lift the armrest for extra wiggle room.

Front of the plane vs. back of the plane

If you’re the type who picks the front of the cabin, you might just be a planner who wants a quick, no-drama exit. Or, Sydney adds, you might have some flying anxiety and prefer to be closer to the pilot and flight attendants. Passengers toward the back, meanwhile, tend to be more laid-back about the whole flying process—or they’re traveling with kids and want to be near the galley and lavatories.

Sitting with your kids (or very deliberately not)

Families don’t always sit shoulder to shoulder, and it’s not because they don’t love each other. Yes, your suspicion is true: Some parents purposely seat their kids in a separate row so they can have some peace and space on the ride. While that’s a terrible idea for little ones, as a mom, I can attest that teens often prefer that arrangement as much as their parents.

But here’s something that surprised me: Sydney says whole families do tend to cluster together in one section of the plane. “At Southwest, we get more of the families in the middle,” she says. “I don’t really know why, but they tend to just kind of flock to the middle of the airplane.”

What else are flight attendants on the lookout for?

Beyond the obvious aisle-versus-window divide, flight attendants have a lot of secrets and are quietly clocking a handful of other seating-adjacent behaviors throughout the flight. For instance, bare feet propped up on the seat, the tray table or the armrest between the seats in front (ew!) says that you don’t care about other people’s comfort and may be socially oblivious. (Thankfully, Sydney says she’s seen less of that in recent years.)

She’s also tuned in to how people react when they end up in the wrong seat entirely, whether by mistake or on purpose, hoping nobody will notice. There are some terrible people who will be assigned a middle seat but claim the window seat, put on headphones and ignore the true seat owner—hoping that they’ll be too afraid of making a scene to claim their spot. “Yes, that happens,” she confirms. “But more often it is an accident when someone is in the wrong seat.”

Her advice is to not be shy about speaking up when something’s bothering you—crew members would honestly rather help sort it out than have you stew in silence for the whole flight.

What do flight attendants do with all this information?

Mostly, this people-watching helps flight attendants be better at their jobs by anticipating needs before passengers even have to ask, which makes the whole flight smoother for everyone. If crew members can predict that the exit row will need an extra safety briefing, that the family in the middle section will need help wrangling a toddler, or that the guy in seat 14C is going to want his laptop out the second the seatbelt sign turns off, they can plan their service accordingly.

There’s a financial angle too. Understanding who tends to spend money on board, and where, helps crew anticipate service needs during the flight. And honestly, even without the practical benefits, it’s clear these flight attendants get a genuine kick out of the sociological experiment happening in their cabin every single day. As someone who spends an unreasonable amount of time analyzing why my own family behaves the way it does on road trips, I respect that immensely.

So the next time you board a flight, just remember: Somebody in a Southwest polo is quietly taking notes, and you are, in fact, an open book.

Sources:
